agreement.heading: What the field agrees on
agreement.body_md: The field generally agrees that AI shows significant potential for applications in medical imaging [doi:10.48550/arxiv.2508.20414]. Federated learning (FL) is considered valuable for medical imaging, primarily because it addresses privacy concerns associated with medical data [doi:10.1016/j.jacr.2022.03.016]. Imaging data is well-suited for FL, as it enables hospitals and devices to jointly train AI/ML models on diverse ultrasound data without exchanging raw scans [doi:10.1007/s11831-026-10629-0]. While many prior works have used simple neural networks like MLPs or shallow CNNs, which may be insufficient for the complexity of medical image classification, researchers are actively performing comprehensive evaluations of state-of-the-art FL algorithms and introducing new optimization approaches to improve performance and applicability in medical imaging [arxiv:2504.05238]. Despite these advancements, identified challenges include performance bottlenecks, heterogeneity risks, and a lack of clinical deployment benchmarks in FL for medical imaging [doi:10.1007/s10462-025-11489-z].

methodology_timeline.heading: Methods and datasets over time
methodology_timeline.body_md: In 2025, the papers [arxiv:2504.05238] and [doi:10.1109/jbhi.2025.3631706] commonly utilized several methods and datasets. Both papers employed "global aggregation" and "federated learning" as key methodologies, alongside the use of a "global classification model" and scenarios involving a "limited local training dataset". Regarding datasets, both works focused on "federated learning" environments, specifically incorporating "unique image datasets", "heterogeneous datasets", and "client local dataset" configurations.
